analysis.one_liner: Lets hospitals and independent technicians repair medical equipment during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The right-to-repair bill died without ever getting a vote: it sat in two House committees from August 2020 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the declared COVID-19 emergency, hospitals and repair shops often cannot fix their own ventilators, imaging machines, and other medical equipment because manufacturers lock the equipment with software and service contracts. This bill would have suspended those barriers for the duration of the emergency, letting hospitals make copies of repair manuals, bypass digital locks to service their machines, and fabricate needed parts on a noncommercial basis. It would also have permanently required manufacturers to sell repair tools and share service information on the same terms they give their own authorized repairers, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals, clinics, and their patients benefit: a broken ventilator or imaging machine could be fixed in days rather than weeks waiting for an authorized manufacturer technician, which matters most when hospitals are overloaded during an emergency. Independent repair businesses and aftermarket tool makers also gain access to a market that manufacturers currently keep to themselves. The FTC gains authority to police manufacturers that refuse to share service information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospitals, patients, and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: During the COVID-19 emergency it would not be copyright infringement for an owner of service manuals or diagnostic software to copy them when needed to repair medical equipment [S2].
It would allow hospitals to bypass digital locks that manufacturers use to restrict access to repair functions, and to make or share the tools that do so [S2].
It would let a hospital fabricate a patented part on a noncommercial basis to keep its own equipment running during the emergency [S2].
It would nullify any purchase or service contract provision that blocks a hospital from repairing its own equipment during the emergency [S2].

It would require manufacturers to sell diagnostic and repair tools and share service information with any owner or independent repairer on terms no worse than those given to authorized repair facilities, with the FTC enforcing the requirement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of medical devices and hospital equipment pay: they would lose control over who repairs their machines, face competition for repair services and replacement parts they currently monopolize, and be required to hand over service documentation and sell their diagnostic tools to independent competitors. Trade secret disclosures are limited to what is already shared with authorized dealers [S3], but the permanent service-information mandate still cuts into a lucrative service-revenue stream.

drawbacks.text: Mandating that manufacturers share diagnostic software and sell repair tools to anyone raises the risk that the information could be used to modify equipment in ways that compromise patient safety, which is why manufacturers argue tightly controlled servicing protects patients [S3].

The bill's scope is tied to the specific COVID-19 emergency declaration for its copyright, patent, and contract provisions, so most of its protections would lapse when the declaration ends, and the manufacturer service mandate is enforced only by the FTC, giving hospitals no direct right to sue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and time-sensitive: when a hospital's ventilator or imaging machine fails during a pandemic, waiting on a single manufacturer-authorized repair channel can mean lost treatment capacity and lives. The safety concerns about untrained repairs are addressed by the bill's limits — it applies only to restoring equipment to original specifications, exempts genuine trade secrets, and leaves all other safety and regulatory laws intact. The bill is narrow and designed around an emergency, which makes its costs modest relative to what it would unlock.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2020 and referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette Clarke introduced the bill on August 7, 2020, during the COVID-19 public health emergency, with Rep. Jerry McNerney as its other original supporter [S1].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever taken: there was no committee vote, no floor vote, and no hearing in the record, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors besides its sponsor, both Democrats, and no companion measure moved in the Senate in the provided record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical device and hospital equipment manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they keep their exclusive control over who can service and repair the machines hospitals depend on, and the service-contract and parts revenue that comes with it. Hospitals remain dependent on manufacturer repair channels for now, though later FTC action and a separate copyright exemption for medical device repair have since chipped at the same problem.

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for letting hospitals repair their own medical equipment during the COVID-19 emergency.

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only other original supporter at introduction.

for.name: 2 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other member signed on before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received a concurrent referral and never took the bill up before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no recorded opposition ever appeared, so the partisan shape of the fight was never tested.

industries.industry: Medical device and hospital equipment manufacturers
industries.note: Manufacturers currently control the repair channel for the machines hospitals buy, through software locks, restrictive service contracts, and proprietary tools — a lucrative service-revenue stream. The bill would have opened that channel to hospitals and independent repairers during the emergency and permanently required fair-terms sharing of service information, costing manufacturers revenue and pricing power while shortening hospital downtime.

industries.industry: Independent medical equipment repair services and aftermarket tool makers
industries.note: The bill would let independent shops service equipment that manufacturers currently restrict to authorized dealers, and would require manufacturers to share the information needed to build competing diagnostic tools. Their gain is hospitals' faster, often cheaper repairs.
